quote: in dem so construirten {+Riemann'schen+}[?] Raume eine Funktion existirt, welche {+überall+} stetig und eindeutig ist?
english: [whether,] in the (Riemannian) space so constructed [by gluing along the cut surfaces], a function exists which is everywhere continuous and single-valued?
topic: Hilbert asks whether a function exists that is continuous and single-valued everywhere in a space constructed by gluing along cut surfaces, and takes as the simplest example 3-dimensional space containing a closed curve with a simple knot, regarded as a branching locus of period 2, which must be cut to make the space simply connected.

triage.modern_statement: Take S^3 (or R^3) and a knotted closed curve K in it, e.g. a trefoil. Cut along a surface bounded by K, glue two copies along the cut, and call the result the 2-fold cyclic branched covering Σ_2(K): the 3-dimensional analogue of a Riemann surface, then called a 'Riemann space'. Hilbert asks whether this space carries a function that is single-valued and continuous everywhere, including on the branch curve. Put another way: is the glued space a proper closed 3-manifold that supports single-valued functions, the way a Riemann surface supports meromorphic functions, and can such functions be built from multivalued functions on R^3 branched along K? The note does not say what extra property the function should have (harmonic, potential-theoretic, etc.). If it only has to be continuous, the question is close to trivial once the space is known to be a manifold. If something like a 3D Riemann existence theorem is meant, the note is too short to say exactly which one.
triage.answered_by: The underlying construction was worked out in the decade after the note. Poul Heegaard (Copenhagen dissertation, 1898) built the 2-fold branched cover of S^3 along the trefoil and identified it, in modern terms, as the lens space L(3,1), a closed 3-manifold. Wilhelm Wirtinger (1905) and Heinrich Tietze (1908) studied branched coverings along knots as 'Riemann spaces'. J. W. Alexander ('Note on Riemann spaces', Bull. AMS 26, 1920) proved that every closed orientable triangulable manifold is a branched covering of the sphere. Hugh Hilden and José María Montesinos later showed that a 3-fold covering branched along a knot always suffices in dimension 3. I found no source that answers Hilbert's exact wording about a function.

evidence.claim: In his 1898 Copenhagen dissertation Heegaard constructed the 2-fold branched cover of the trefoil and showed that it is a lens space.

Heegaard found that the double cover of S^3 branched over a trefoil brings an extra ingredient into 3-dimensional homology. This is presented as the analogue of getting Riemann surfaces by covering S^2.
English translation of Heegaard's thesis. It discusses branch lines in 3-dimensional coverings by analogy with branch points on Riemann surfaces.

Wirtinger presented coverings branched along knots (from the study of algebraic functions) to the 1905 annual meeting. The covering in question turned out to be a 3-sheeted covering branched along the trefoil.

Heegaard's cover was used to build 'Riemann spaces', the analogue of Riemann surfaces. The knot-classification problem was not his interest and was only solved by Tietze in 1908 using the fundamental group.
Alexander (1920) showed that every closed orientable triangulated 3-manifold is a cover of S^3 branched along the 1-skeleton of a tetrahedron.
Every closed orientable 3-manifold is a 3-fold branched covering of S^3 (Hilden; branched along a knot). The paper cites Alexander, 'Note on Riemann spaces'.

triage.why: The page describes the topic now called cyclic branched coverings of S^3 along knots, Hilbert's 'Riemann spaces'. It uses exactly the example Heegaard published in 1898: the 2-fold cover branched along the trefoil, which turns out to be the lens space L(3,1). Wirtinger, Tietze and Alexander (1905–1920) developed this into standard 3-manifold topology. Because the glued space is a closed manifold, everywhere continuous single-valued functions on it exist, so the literal question is settled. Branched double covers are still actively studied, for example in knot Floer homology. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source that refers to this note. The note is unclear and does not say what property the function must have, so I can't match it to one specific later theorem. That is why confidence is low.
